==Problem==
Two <imath>600</imath> mL pitchers contain orange juice. One pitcher is <imath>1/3</imath> full and the other pitcher is <imath>2/5</imath> full. Water is added to fill each pitcher completely, then both pitchers are poured into one large container. What fraction of the mixture in the large container is orange juice?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ \frac18 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ \frac{3}{16} \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ \frac{11}{30} \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ \frac{11}{19}\qquad \textbf{(E)}\ \frac{11}{15}</imath>

==Solution 1==
The first pitcher contains <imath>600 \cdot \frac13 = 200</imath> mL of orange juice. The second pitcher contains <imath>600 \cdot \frac25 = 240</imath> mL of orange juice. In the large pitcher, there is a total of <imath>200+240=440</imath> mL of orange juice and <imath>600+600=1200</imath> mL of fluids, giving a fraction of <imath>\frac{440}{1200} = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{11}{30}}</imath>.

==Solution 2==
We have the first pitcher having <imath>\frac13</imath> orange juice, and the other having <imath>\frac25</imath>, so we can simply add together the fractions and get <imath>\frac{11}{15}</imath>, but since we poured <imath>2</imath> containers together, so we divide by <imath>2</imath> and get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{11}{30}}</imath>.

~TheRealMee
